title: Manual small-incision cataract surgery (SICS)
subtitle: Sutureless scleral tunnel, nucleus delivery and rigid or foldable implant

sources.title: Safety and efficacy of phacoemulsification compared with manual small-incision cataract surgery by a randomized controlled clinical trial

sources.org: Ruit S et al. Am J Ophthalmol 143:32
sources.title: A prospective randomized clinical trial of phacoemulsification vs manual sutureless small-incision extracapsular cataract surgery in Nepal
Guidelines for prevention and treatment of endophthalmitis following cataract surgery

indications: Visually significant cataract, including dense brunescent, white and mature cataracts where phaco is harder.
High-volume settings: outcomes comparable to phaco in randomised trials, with lower cost and no phaco machine.
contraindications: Active ocular surface or adnexal infection until treated.
A patient who cannot lie flat and still, unless general anaesthesia is arranged.
preparation: Biometry and the implant plan, as for phaco; a back-up implant for the sulcus or anterior chamber.
Check anticoagulants and alpha-blockers; dilate well.
Consent: endophthalmitis, posterior capsule rupture, corneal oedema, astigmatism from the incision, retinal complications, and the need for glasses.
positioning: Supine with the head flat and level, chin and forehead in one horizontal plane, a head ring or gel pillow; the head of the patient at the end of the table so the surgeon can sit.
equipment: Crescent blade, keratome (3.2 mm) and side-port blade, viscoelastic, cystotome, irrigating vectis or Simcoe cannula, rigid PMMA or foldable implant, wet-field cautery, anterior vitrectomy on standby.
anatomy: Superior or temporal bulbar conjunctiva and Tenon's, the sclera 1.5 to 2 mm behind the limbus, the corneal endothelium, the capsule and zonules.
The tunnel runs from sclera into clear cornea, so the internal opening is in cornea and the wound self-seals.
criticalSafety: Right patient, right eye, right implant: read the biometry and the implant aloud.
A tunnel of the right length and depth: too superficial buttonholes, too deep enters the chamber early and leaks.
Protect the endothelium with viscoelastic when the nucleus comes out.
commonErrors: A tunnel too small for the nucleus, which then tears the endothelium on the way out.
Forcing the nucleus out without viscoelastic cover.
complications: Posterior capsule rupture and vitreous loss.
postop: Antibiotic and steroid drops; shield at night.
Same-day return for pain, redness or falling vision.
Refraction at about four to six weeks.

steps.emphasis: Mark the operative eye; confirm the eye with the patient in their own language.
Read the implant model and power aloud; confirm the back-up implant is in the room.
Peribulbar or sub-Tenon block is usual for SICS.
Supine with the head flat and level, chin and forehead in one horizontal plane, a head ring or gel pillow; the head of the patient at the end of the table so the surgeon can sit.
Check the tunnel self-seals; reposit the conjunctival flap over it and cauterise lightly.

step.sics.tunnel.title: Fornix-based conjunctival flap and sclerocorneal tunnel
step.sics.tunnel.why: The tunnel is the whole idea of SICS: a self-sealing, sutureless wound big enough to deliver the nucleus. Its width must match the nucleus and its depth must stay even.
how: Make a small fornix-based conjunctival flap and apply light wet-field cautery to the sclera.
Make a partial-thickness frown or straight external incision about 6 to 7 mm long, 1.5 to 2 mm behind the limbus.
Dissect the tunnel forwards with a crescent blade at even depth, about one third to one half scleral thickness, 1 to 1.5 mm into clear cornea, widening the internal end like a funnel.
Make a side port, fill the chamber with viscoelastic and enter the chamber with a keratome at the end of the tunnel.
pitfalls: Entering the chamber before the end of the tunnel, so the wound leaks.
A tunnel too narrow for a hard nucleus.

step.sics.capsulotomy.title: Anterior capsulotomy
step.sics.capsulotomy.why: The nucleus has to come out of the bag, so the opening must be large enough to let it prolapse without tearing round to the posterior capsule.
how: Under viscoelastic, perform a large continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis (about 6 to 7 mm) with relaxing cuts if needed, or a can-opener capsulotomy in a white cataract.
Stain the capsule with trypan blue when the red reflex is poor.
pitfalls: A small rhexis that traps the nucleus.

step.sics.prolapse.title: Hydrodissection and prolapsing the nucleus into the chamber
step.sics.prolapse.why: Bringing the nucleus out of the bag into the anterior chamber, rather than levering it out from the bag, keeps the posterior capsule and zonules safe.
how: Hydrodissect until the nucleus is free; with a large rhexis, one pole can be prolapsed with the fluid wave.
Rotate or dial the nucleus out of the bag into the anterior chamber.
Inject viscoelastic above and below it to protect the endothelium and push the posterior capsule back.
pitfalls: Forcing a nucleus through a small rhexis.
Working with no viscoelastic cushion over the endothelium.

step.sics.delivery.title: Delivering the nucleus through the tunnel
step.sics.delivery.why: Delivery is the step that can damage the endothelium or tear the iris if the tunnel is too small or the nucleus is pushed rather than guided.
how: Slide an irrigating vectis under the nucleus, or use viscoexpression or the fish-hook technique per training.
Apply gentle pressure on the posterior lip of the tunnel so the nucleus glides out with the fluid.
Enlarge the tunnel rather than force a nucleus that will not pass.
pitfalls: Forcing a large nucleus through a small tunnel.
Pressing on the globe with an open tunnel.

step.sics.cortex-iol.title: Cortex aspiration and implant insertion
step.sics.cortex-iol.why: Clean cortex removal and an implant centred in the bag decide the final vision and the long-term stability.
how: Aspirate cortex with a Simcoe cannula or an irrigation-aspiration system, port facing up.
Fill the bag with viscoelastic and place the implant in the bag; dial it centred.
Wash out the viscoelastic and form the chamber with balanced salt.
pitfalls: An implant left half in the sulcus.
